sm: Host Kate Odell opens with two stories: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth surviving an impeachment effort, and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang's admitted affair with a business customer who has alleged ties to the Chinese government. The House voted two hundred eleven to two hundred four on Tuesday to send Republican Thomas Massie's charges back to the Judiciary Committee, which effectively kills them for this Congress. Eleven Democrats did not vote, and they blamed a traffic jam, even though Hakeem Jeffries had called himself a hard yes. Matt Continetti says it embarrasses Jeffries somewhat, but that the incoming Democratic majority will be big and mostly mainstream liberal. He also notes Republican unity, including the choice of Jim Jordan as minority leader. Both hosts praise Hegseth's Tuesday press conference, where he called the effort a stunt and cited the lack of impeachments over Lloyd Austin.

Joe Sternberg says impeachment is a political process, and Hegseth's press conference was a warning to Democrats that he and the administration will mount an aggressive political defense rather than argue legal details. He adds that Hegseth is a poor scapegoat for the Iran war, since the president made the decision and the military has limited the fallout by being competent. Matt Continetti then assesses the articles themselves. He says they lack any specific high crime and amount to impeaching Hegseth for every Trump foreign policy move, from the Houthi strikes to the capture of Maduro and the Iran operations. The one real legal debate, he says, concerns strikes on suspected drug boats and whether the cartels count as enemy forces. He calls the resolution a partisan act and wonders whether Democrats will revive a narrower version next year.

Joe Sternberg says Hegseth survived, but the vote looked close, and many retiring Republican senators are unhappy with Trump, including Cornyn, Tillis and Joni Ernst. He argues that more impeachments would distract Democrats from building an economic agenda for 2028, though pressure from their base may make it hard to resist. Kate Odell says the effort revived Hegseth's standing, and Trump rarely concedes to Democrats under pressure. Matt Continetti says Trump is staying the course. He replaced Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, and he is keeping the naval blockade of Iran and adding Operation Iron Gate to stop overland smuggling. Continetti welcomed the press conference as a real argument for Trump's foreign policy and the reforms at the Pentagon, such as record recruiting. He says Hegseth should be more accessible to the press and to Republicans on Capitol Hill.

The conversation turns to Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, who is not related to him and whose company has alleged ties to the Chinese government. Nvidia's board says it will investigate and denies that any national secrets are at risk. Joe Sternberg says it is not clear she is a spy. He describes a murky Chinese business world in which people have vague links to the state that can create vulnerabilities. Her Singaporean company reportedly rented data center space in Southeast Asia, which let Chinese firms get around chip export controls, and he expects the scandal to bring that issue to the public. Kate Odell points to China's military-civil fusion strategy. Matt Continetti doubts it will change Trump's approach to his upcoming meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, noting Trump has stood by Huang. He calls this the fifth major example of Chinese infiltration.

Matt Continetti lists earlier cases, including the Arcadia, California mayor who resigned, a driver for the late Senator Feinstein, and a former aide to New York Governor Kathy Hochul. He says the scandal could harden export controls on chips, and a Democratic Congress will likely push tough limits like Biden's. Kate Odell asks about the argument that selling chips makes China dependent on the United States. Joe Sternberg says the argument will not work, since China has always caught up or stolen new technology, and Beijing does not plan to depend on American hardware. He says the anti-data-center movement needs no help from this scandal. He adds that the case shows how hard it is to know who you are dealing with in Chinese business, where fixers hide beneficial ownership. Odell ends by noting that House Republicans have asked Jensen Huang for a briefing.
